claims.text: A hybrid ab initio and machine-learning framework can incorporate corrections for oxygen defect-induced scattering.
The framework can incorporate anharmonic lattice effects.
The framework will predict the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen within ±15% of experiment over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The initial material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Training on oxygen-defect configurations and their local electronic and vibrational properties can correct conventional DFT-based conductivity predictions.
The simulations will incorporate electronic-temperature effects over the specified temperature ranges.
The simulations will incorporate anharmonic lattice vibrations over the specified temperature ranges.
Oxygen impurities locally modify the electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurities modify defect–phonon interactions and associated scattering rates.
Defect clustering and anharmonic effects produce variations in scattering rates.
An ML model trained on defective-cell ab initio data can learn corrections for defect-induced and anharmonic effects.
Applying the learned correction to an analytical conductivity model will improve predictive accuracy across both target temperature regimes.
The enhanced model is expected to reduce prediction error by more than 20% relative to standard defect-free models.
A held-out 800 K conductivity prediction for a specimen containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen that differs from experiment by more than 15% will falsify the hypothesis.
Perfect-crystal DFT-based analytical conductivity models typically have errors exceeding ±20% for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
The proposed model is intended to apply only over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to specimens with oxygen content near 1 wt.%.
Accuracy may degrade outside the stated temperature and oxygen-content ranges because of training-data sparsity and inadequately captured long-range defect correlations.
The quantitative improvement depends on the diversity and accuracy of the ab initio training data.
Incomplete treatment of long-range defect interactions and anharmonic effects could affect predictions near the extremes of the target temperature ranges.
Validation will compare model predictions against an independent, held-out electrical-conductivity measurement at 800 K for a specimen with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
